props.sub: four more behavioral questions · with full worked answers · Senior EM

props.title: Measuring team performance
props.q: How do you measure your team's performance?

moves.title: Reject vanity metrics
moves.desc: Velocity and lines of code measure motion, not impact. Don't lead with them.

moves.title: Measure outcomes
moves.desc: Tie the team to business and user outcomes — did the work move the needle?

moves.title: Track delivery health
moves.desc: The DORA metrics: deploy frequency, lead time, change-fail rate, time to restore.

moves.title: Watch the humans
moves.desc: Retention, on-call load, and eNPS. Hitting numbers while burning out is failing.

props.trap: “We track story points and velocity.” That rewards busywork, not value.
props.signal: You manage outcomes and team health, not activity theater.
props.foot: Great managers measure whether the work mattered — and whether the team can keep doing it.

props.title: When the velocity chart lied
props.situation: I inherited a team whose velocity chart looked fantastic — story points up and to the right. But leadership was frustrated, features weren't really landing, and two engineers were quietly interviewing elsewhere.
props.task: My mandate: figure out why a supposedly high-performing team wasn't actually delivering.

actions.d: Ignored the vanity metrics and instrumented what mattered — the DORA metrics and real feature outcomes.
Found the truth: lead time was three weeks, change-fail rate was 30%, and on-call was brutal.
Refocused the team on outcomes and reliability, and made lead time and deploy frequency the visible goals.
Added a lightweight team-health pulse, so morale was a number I watched, not a surprise.

props.learning: Velocity measures motion. Outcomes, reliability, and team health measure performance.
props.foot: You looked past the flattering chart to what the team actually produced. That's judgment.

props.title: Re-energizing a demoralized team
props.q: How do you motivate a team that has lost its motivation?

moves.title: Find the real cause
moves.desc: Burnout, a failed launch, no autonomy, unclear purpose? Diagnose, don't cheerlead.

moves.title: Restore meaning and wins
moves.desc: Reconnect the work to real impact, and engineer a few early, visible wins.

moves.title: Give autonomy back
moves.desc: Remove the blockers and the thrash; let them own decisions again.

moves.title: Fix the system
moves.desc: Repair whatever burned them out, or morale just slides back to zero.

props.trap: You threw a pizza party or a speech at a structural problem.
props.signal: You treat morale as a system to diagnose and fix, not a mood to hype.
props.foot: Motivation is a symptom. You fix the cause — purpose, autonomy, and a sane pace.

props.title: The team that survived a death march
props.situation: I took over a team right after a brutal six-month death march — nights and weekends — to ship a launch that then got cancelled. Morale was on the floor, velocity had collapsed, and cynicism was everywhere.
props.task: My mandate: rebuild the team's energy and output, without another forced march.

actions.d: Started by listening — one-on-ones with everyone, no agenda, just what's broken and what they'd change.
Reconnected them to impact — killed the low-value work and picked a project with real, visible user value.
Engineered early wins — shipped something small but real in two weeks to rebuild belief.
Fixed the cause — capped the hours, protected focus time, and gave decisions back to the team.

props.learning: You can't pep-talk your way out of burnout. Remove the cause, then rebuild belief with wins.
props.foot: You diagnosed the cause and rebuilt trust with action, not slogans. That's leadership.

props.title: Retaining a key engineer
props.q: A key engineer says they're thinking of leaving. Now what?

moves.title: Understand the real reason
moves.desc: Money, growth, manager, boredom, burnout? The stated reason is rarely the whole one.

moves.title: Act on what you can
moves.desc: Fix growth, scope, or recognition fast; be honest about what you can't change.

moves.title: Make a genuine case
moves.desc: A specific future here — not a panic counter-offer that resets in six months.

moves.title: Learn from every exit
moves.desc: If they still go, run an honest retro and fix the pattern for the rest.

props.trap: You only reacted with a counter-offer once they'd already mentally quit.
props.signal: You retain people through growth and trust, and handle regretted attrition with grace.
props.foot: The best retention happens months before the resignation — but you can still save some.

props.title: The star engineer with one foot out the door
props.situation: My strongest engineer, Ana — the one who owned our core service — asked for a private one-on-one and told me she'd started interviewing. Losing her would have set the team back a year.
props.task: My mandate: understand why, and keep her — but only if staying was genuinely right for her.

actions.d: Listened first, didn't panic — and the real reason wasn't pay. She felt stuck and unchallenged.
Acted fast on what I could — carved out a new architecture charter that stretched her, within two weeks.
Made a specific, honest case for her future here, instead of a desperate counter-offer.
Fixed the root cause for others too — I'd under-invested in growth across all my senior engineers.

props.learning: Retention is built months early through growth. A counter-offer alone just delays the exit.
props.foot: You addressed the real cause, not the symptom — and fixed it for the whole team.

props.title: Managing managers, and scaling yourself
props.q: How do you lead when you're managing managers, not engineers?

moves.title: Change what you optimize
moves.desc: You no longer ship features. You ship healthy teams and good managers.

moves.title: Delegate outcomes, not tasks
moves.desc: Set the what and the why; let them own the how, and the mistakes.

moves.title: Use skip-levels and signals
moves.desc: Skip-level one-on-ones and team-health metrics — lead through, not around, your managers.

moves.title: Grow your managers
moves.desc: Coach them like you once coached engineers. Your leverage is their growth.

props.trap: You kept operating like a lead — in the code, in the details, undermining your managers.
props.signal: You lead through others and scale your impact past what you could do alone.
props.foot: The job stops being about your output, and starts being about your leaders' output.

props.title: Turning a great engineer into a first-time manager
props.situation: As my org grew past twenty people, I had to split it into teams. My strongest tech lead, Ravi, was the obvious choice to run one — but he'd never managed, and great engineers often make miserable managers.
props.task: My mandate: grow Ravi into a real manager, without losing him or breaking his team.

actions.d: Set the new bar explicitly — his job was now his team's output and growth, not his own commits.
Delegated outcomes, not tasks — I gave him the goals and let him own the how, including early mistakes.
Coached him weekly on the craft — feedback, prioritization, one-on-ones — and used skip-levels to sense the team without going around him.
Protected his authority — I let his team see him as the decision-maker, and backed his calls in public.

props.learning: Managing managers means coaching the craft and leading through them, never around them.
props.foot: You scaled yourself by growing a leader, not by staying the hero engineer. The senior bar.

items: Measure outcomes and team health, never just velocity.
Motivation is a system — fix the cause, don't throw a party.
Retain people through growth, months before they quit.
Managing managers means leading through them, not around.
Same spine every time: STAR, plus what you learned.
props.closer: Lead the team, grow the leaders, and the output takes care of itself.
